definition: Encryption and decryption use a shared secret key. Symmetric schemes commonly protect bulk data; the particular mode determines authentication, nonce and length requirements.
example: A laptop disk may use a storage mode such as XTS, while TLS 1.3 records use a specified AEAD; AES-GCM is not a universal disk-encryption mode.

definition: A secret cryptographic value used by a specified algorithm, such as a symmetric cipher or MAC. Suitable length, randomness and protection depend on that algorithm; bit length alone does not establish effective security.
example: An AES-256 key is 32 random bytes, giving 2^256 possible keys.

definition: The output of encryption. What it reveals depends on the scheme and its correct use: secure application encryption aims to hide plaintext content while permitting specified leakage such as length. Ciphertext alone does not imply integrity.
example: AES-GCM turns a 10-byte plaintext into 10 bytes of ciphertext plus a 16-byte tag.

definition: A keyed function that encrypts fixed-size blocks: for each key it maps every possible input block to a unique output block, and should look like a random permutation to anyone without the key. AES has 128-bit (16-byte) blocks.
example: Encrypting a 1 MB file with AES needs a mode of operation, because AES itself only handles 16 bytes at a time.

definition: The block cipher designed by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen that NIST selected in 2000 and standardised as AES. AES is Rijndael restricted to 128-bit blocks.
One repetition of a cipher’s round transformation. AES has 10, 12 or 14 rounds after an initial round-key addition; its final round omits the column-mixing operation.
example: AES-128 has ten rounds, with MixColumns in its first nine rounds.

definition: Federal Information Processing Standards are US federal standards published by NIST. They include cryptographic algorithm specifications and FIPS 140 requirements for cryptographic modules; choosing one approved algorithm alone does not validate an entire application.
example: A government contract may require "FIPS-validated" cryptography, meaning a module tested under FIPS 140.

definition: NIST's Special Publication 800 series: detailed security guidance and standards, such as SP 800-38D (the GCM mode), SP 800-57 (key management and key-size equivalences) and SP 800-185 (KMAC).
example: SP 800-38D limits random 96-bit GCM nonces to 2^32 messages per key.

definition: A quantum search algorithm that finds a marked item among N possibilities in about √N queries instead of about N/2. Against a k-bit key it suggests roughly 2^(k/2) quantum queries, which is why AES-256 is seen as a comfortable post-quantum margin.
example: Ideal Grover search against AES-128 would need on the order of 2^64 queries; real quantum runtimes would be far higher.

definition: AES New Instructions: an x86 instruction-set extension that accelerates AES transformations. Arm has separate cryptographic instruction extensions; a hardware AES operation can avoid secret-indexed table accesses but does not make an entire protocol side-channel safe.
example: Hardware and library support affect whether AES-GCM or another AEAD is faster; benchmark the actual device.

definition: A construction that uses a block cipher to process messages, defining how blocks are encrypted or combined with counters and, for authenticated modes, how authentication is computed. ECB, CBC, CTR and GCM are examples.
example: AES-GCM means AES used in Galois/Counter Mode.

definition: Electronic Codebook mode encrypts each fixed-size block independently under one key. Its block size is that of the underlying cipher: 16 bytes for AES. Equal plaintext blocks reveal equality through equal ciphertext blocks, so it is unsuitable for ordinary structured application data.
example: The "ECB penguin": an image encrypted with ECB still shows the penguin's outline.

definition: Cipher Block Chaining mode mixes each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, starting with an unpredictable IV. Ordinary CBC handles complete blocks, so variable-length byte strings normally need padding; CBC alone provides no integrity. Revealing padding validity can create an attack oracle.
example: TLS 1.0 used CBC with predictable IVs, which the BEAST attack exploited in 2011.

definition: Counter mode: a block cipher encrypts successive counter blocks (nonce plus counter) to make a keystream, which is XORed with the plaintext. It needs no padding and runs in parallel, but a counter block must never repeat under the same key, and without a MAC it is malleable.
example: AES-GCM uses CTR mode for its encryption part.

definition: Galois/Counter Mode is an authenticated-encryption mode combining counter-mode encryption with GHASH and a nonce-dependent tag mask. It authenticates ciphertext and associated data; reusing a nonce under one key can reveal plaintext relations and enable forgeries.
example: TLS 1.3's TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 suite uses AES-GCM with a 96-bit nonce and a 128-bit tag.

definition: The polynomial hash inside GCM, keyed by a value H derived by encrypting a zero block with the AES key. Combined with a nonce-dependent mask it produces GCM's tag; on its own it is not a secure MAC, and nonce reuse can reveal H.
The authentication-only variant of GCM, which computes a GCM tag over data without encrypting anything. Like GCM it needs a unique nonce per key.

An AEAD specified in RFC 8452 that provides nonce-misuse resistance under its stated bounds. Repetition leaks equality of the complete protected inputs and degrades bounds, but avoids the catastrophic repeated-keystream failure of ordinary GCM. Continue to generate fresh nonces and obey usage limits.
example: Nonce-misuse resistance is a safety margin, not permission to use a fixed nonce indefinitely.

definition: A starting input to a cipher mode, normally public and sent with the ciphertext. Requirements depend on the mode: CBC requires an unpredictable IV, while CTR requires counter blocks that never repeat under one key.
example: AES-CBC uses a 16-byte random IV, stored in front of the ciphertext.

definition: A value with scheme-specific freshness or uniqueness requirements. AEAD nonces are normally public and must follow the algorithm’s per-key uniqueness rules; ECDSA’s secret signing value instead must be generated securely or derived by a specified deterministic procedure. Do not transfer one scheme’s nonce rules to another.
example: Reusing a GCM nonce under one key leaks the XOR of the two plaintexts and can enable forgeries.

definition: The pseudorandom bytes a stream cipher or CTR mode generates from the key and nonce, which are XORed with the plaintext to encrypt. The same key and nonce always give the same keystream.
example: If two messages share a keystream, XORing their ciphertexts gives the XOR of their plaintexts.

definition: A cipher that encrypts by XORing the plaintext with a keystream, byte by byte, so ciphertext is the same length as plaintext. ChaCha20 is a stream cipher; CTR mode turns a block cipher into one.

Exclusive or, written ⊕: a bitwise operation whose output bit is 1 where the two input bits differ and 0 where they match. XORing the same value twice cancels it, which is why it both applies and removes a keystream.
example: 0x31 ⊕ 0x37 = 0x06, because the two bytes differ in exactly two bit positions.

definition: Reusing one keystream to encrypt distinct plaintexts. XORing the ciphertexts exposes the XOR of the corresponding plaintext bytes; known or correctly guessed bytes reveal the matching bytes of the other message, not necessarily both complete messages.
example: Reusing an AES-CTR key and nonce turns it into a two-time pad.

definition: A byte-padding rule used with block ciphers: append between one byte and a complete block, each byte equal to the count appended. For AES the block size is 16 bytes; an already aligned input receives a full block. Revealing whether validation succeeds can create a padding oracle.
example: A 10-byte message gets six 0x06 bytes; a 16-byte message gets a whole extra block of 0x10.

definition: A system that reveals, through an error message, status code or timing difference, whether a decrypted message had valid padding. An attacker can submit modified ciphertexts and use the answers to decrypt CBC data byte by byte without the key.
example: Returning "invalid padding" (400) for some tokens and "invalid token" (401) for others is a padding oracle.

definition: A 2013 timing attack on TLS and DTLS CBC cipher suites: tiny differences in MAC-checking time, depending on the padding, acted as a padding oracle even when error messages were identical.

"Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption" (2014): an attack that forced connections down to SSL 3.0 and then exploited its loosely checked CBC padding to decrypt data such as cookies. It led to SSL 3.0 being disabled.

"Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS" (2011): an attack on TLS 1.0 CBC, which used the last ciphertext block of one record as the IV of the next, making IVs predictable. It recovered secrets such as cookies.
A weakness where an attacker can change a ciphertext so that it decrypts to a predictably related plaintext, without knowing the key. Unauthenticated stream modes and textbook RSA are malleable.
example: Flipping one ciphertext bit in AES-CTR flips the same plaintext bit, turning "pay Bob 10" into "pay Bob 90".

definition: Encryption with authentication, providing confidentiality and a check for unauthorised changes under the scheme’s assumptions and usage bounds. AEAD additionally authenticates associated data without hiding it; a safe decrypt API reports authentication failure before releasing usable plaintext. Forgery probability is small rather than mathematically zero.
example: AES-GCM decryption raises InvalidTag when its authentication check fails; successful forgery has a nonzero probability governed by the scheme and usage bounds.

definition: Data authenticated by an AEAD but left unencrypted, such as a record header. The receiver supplies the expected bytes; changing them affects verification, with security subject to the scheme’s forgery bounds. AAD is not confidential.
example: Passing b"order-id:4711" as associated data stops an attacker moving a ciphertext onto a different order.

definition: The short value a MAC or AEAD computes over the message (and key) so the receiver can detect changes. It is typically 16 bytes (128 bits); shorter tags make guessing a valid tag easier.
example: An HMAC-SHA256 tag is 32 bytes, often sent as 64 hex characters.

definition: A fast stream cipher designed by Daniel J. Bernstein, standardised for IETF use in RFC 8439. It runs quickly in software on devices without AES hardware.
A fast one-time MAC: each key must authenticate only one message. ChaCha20-Poly1305 derives a fresh Poly1305 key for every nonce.

An AEAD (RFC 8439) combining the ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 MAC, with a 96-bit nonce and a 128-bit tag. It is the usual alternative to AES-GCM, especially on phones without AES instructions.
example: TLS 1.3 and WireGuard both use ChaCha20-Poly1305.

definition: A ChaCha20-Poly1305 variant with a 192-bit nonce, large enough that randomly chosen nonces practically never collide. It is not nonce-misuse resistant: a repeated nonce is still a serious failure.
example: libsodium offers XChaCha20-Poly1305 so applications can safely use random nonces for huge message counts.

definition: A high-level authenticated-encryption recipe in Python's cryptography library: AES-128-CBC with HMAC-SHA256, a random IV and a timestamp, packed into a single token. It has no associated-data input.

A cryptography library derived from the distinct NaCl library. Its secretbox API performs authenticated symmetric encryption; the caller supplies a nonce and must follow the algorithm’s nonce requirements.

Google’s cryptography library offering high-level primitives and key-management APIs intended to reduce common misuse. Security and nonce-misuse properties depend on the selected primitive and correct integration.

For independent uniform samples from N possible values, collisions become appreciable around the square root of N samples because the number of pairs grows quadratically. Thus an ideal n-bit hash has roughly n/2-bit generic classical collision strength.
example: Under the uniform independent birthday model, 23 people give about a 50.7% chance of a match; a uniform 64-bit identifier space reaches about 50% after 5 billion samples.

definition: Producing an accepted authentication tag or digital signature for a new message without the required secret authority. Secure constructions make this computationally infeasible within their security bounds; a guessed tag can still succeed with nonzero probability.
The property that changing any one input bit flips about half the output bits, unpredictably. It is why "abc" and "abd" have completely unrelated SHA-256 digests.

The intended computational difficulty of finding an input matching a given digest. An ideal hash with an n-bit output has a generic preimage-search cost on the scale of the full output space; small candidate dictionaries can be tested directly.

The intended computational difficulty of finding a different input with the same digest as a particular given input. Generic ideal-hash estimates assume appropriate message-length and input models; they are not universal guarantees for every construction or very long message.

The intended computational difficulty of finding any two distinct inputs with equal digests. An ideal n-bit hash offers roughly n/2 bits of generic classical collision strength through the birthday bound; concrete weak hashes may be much easier to attack.
example: SHAttered broke SHA-1's collision resistance in 2017 with about 2^63 computations.

definition: If more items than boxes are placed into boxes, some box holds at least two. Since a hash has more possible inputs than outputs, collisions must exist; security only requires that they are infeasible to find.

A construction that pads a message and processes its blocks through a compression function with a running chaining state. Full-state output variants such as SHA-256 reveal that final state and permit classic length extension; truncated variants do not expose it all.
The fixed-size building block of a Merkle–Damgård hash: it takes the current chaining value and one message block and outputs a new chaining value of the same size.
example: SHA-256's compression function takes a 256-bit state and a 512-bit block.

definition: The running value a hash function carries from block to block. In MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512 the final internal state is the digest itself, which is what lets attackers resume hashing (length extension).

For full-state chaining hashes such as SHA-256, a known digest and input length let an attacker compute a digest for the original bytes, their hash padding and chosen extra data. A secret-prefix MAC can therefore be forged after guessing the secret length; parser acceptance is a separate requirement. HMAC avoids this construction.
example: An API that signed requests as MD5(secret ‖ params) let attackers append &admin=true with a valid tag.

definition: The design behind SHA-3: input is absorbed into a large internal state, and output is squeezed out of only part of it. Because the digest never reveals the whole state, it resists length extension.

The NIST hash family (FIPS 180-4) including SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 and the truncated SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256. It is the workhorse of TLS, code signing and package managers, and remains secure.

The NIST FIPS 202 hash standard, published in 2015, based on Keccak’s sponge construction and structurally different from SHA-2. SHA-3 does not expose the full chaining state used by classic Merkle–Damgård length-extension attacks. Ethereum’s Keccak-256 differs from SHA3-256.
A fast hash family (RFC 7693): BLAKE2b produces up to 512 bits and BLAKE2s up to 256. It has a built-in key parameter, so keyed BLAKE2 works as a MAC, and it resists length extension.
example: WireGuard uses BLAKE2s.

definition: A 2020 successor to BLAKE2 designed for high speed and parallelism, with a 256-bit default output that can be extended to a requested length within the specification and implementation limits.
A hash-like function that can produce output of any requested length, such as SHAKE (from SHA-3) or BLAKE3. Longer output does not raise security beyond the function's design strength.
The 2017 attack by Google and CWI Amsterdam that produced two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 digest, the first public SHA-1 collision. It took about 2^63 SHA-1 computations.
Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, the Dutch national research institute for mathematics and computer science, co-author of the SHAttered SHA-1 collision.

A stronger collision attack where the attacker picks two different starting documents and then computes suffixes that make the full documents hash the same. It enables forged certificates; such attacks exist for MD5 and SHA-1.
Espionage malware discovered in 2012 that used an MD5 chosen-prefix collision to forge a Microsoft code-signing certificate, so Windows Update trusted its fake updates.

Identifying content using a digest or a structured identifier containing a digest. Recomputing the digest helps check content against an expected identifier, subject to hash security; it does not itself establish publisher identity or availability.

A digest identifies a container image manifest or index by its content. Pulling a trusted digest pins that object and its referenced content under the hash assumptions; the digest alone does not authenticate a publisher.
example: An image index can reference different platform-specific manifests, so one index digest does not mean every platform executes identical files.

definition: The InterPlanetary File System, a peer-to-peer system using content identifiers (CIDs) for blocks and linked data. A file’s CID can identify a structured DAG rather than being the hash of the raw file bytes; chunking and encoding affect it.

A hash tree in which parent hashes commit to their children. In a complete balanced binary tree, a leaf inclusion path needs one sibling digest per level; proofs also require the specified leaf encoding, ordering and a trusted root.
example: A tree over 1,048,576 items needs only 20 sibling hashes to prove one item is included.

definition: Public append-only certificate logs with cryptographic proofs supporting auditing and monitoring of certificate issuance. They help observers discover suspect issuance; a log entry alone does not determine whether a certificate was authorised by the domain owner.
A cryptocurrency whose blockchain uses SHA-256 (in proof-of-work and Merkle trees of transactions) and ECDSA signatures on the secp256k1 curve.
A blockchain platform that, like Bitcoin, signs transactions with ECDSA over the secp256k1 curve; it hashes with Keccak-256.

A 32-bit cyclic redundancy check: a fast checksum that detects accidental corruption such as transmission errors. Anyone can compute a matching CRC for altered data, so it gives no protection against attackers.
example: Zip files and Ethernet frames carry CRC32 checksums.

definition: A fast hash such as MurmurHash or xxHash designed for hash tables and corruption checks, not for security. An attacker can easily construct collisions or inputs with chosen hashes.

A small value computed from data to detect errors or check integrity. A plain checksum or hash only helps against attackers if the expected value comes from a channel they cannot change, such as a signed checksum file.
Base-16 notation using the digits 0–9 and a–f. Each hex digit stands for 4 bits, so one byte is two hex digits; the prefix 0x marks a hex number.
example: 0x5A is the byte 0101 1010, decimal 90.

definition: Trying candidate secrets from a likely set and checking each against available evidence. A small candidate space can make attacks practical, but the ability to check guesses, password-KDF cost, rate limits and unavailable pepper keys affect feasibility.

Processing that replaces or separates identifying information so attribution needs additional information. It differs from anonymisation: a plain predictable-identifier hash can still be guessed or linked.
example: Hashing a small fixed phone-number format does not make it anonymous.

definition: An open-source ecosystem for signing and verifying software artefacts. Its common keyless flow uses an ephemeral signing key, an identity-bound certificate and transparency logging; “keyless” does not mean that no cryptographic key exists. Other signing modes also exist.
GNU Privacy Guard: a tool implementing the OpenPGP standard, widely used to sign release files and checksums and to encrypt email.
A distributed NoSQL database; its anti-entropy repair compares Merkle trees of replicas to find data that differs.

Message authentication code: a tag computed from a secret key and a message. A suitable scheme supports integrity and key-holder authenticity within its forgery bounds; it does not identify which shared-key holder sent a message or establish freshness or confidentiality.
example: GitHub signs each webhook body with HMAC-SHA256 when you configure a webhook secret.

definition: HMAC uses nested keyed hash applications; HMAC-SHA256 instantiates it with SHA-256 and produces a 32-byte full tag. HMAC-SHA512 is a different instantiation with a 64-byte full tag. Both avoid the secret-prefix length-extension construction.

A security goal that limits an attacker’s probability of producing an accepted tag or signature for a new message after seeing tags or signatures for messages of their choice. The probability and resource bounds depend on the precise construction and definition.
The keyed MAC built on SHA-3's Keccak function, standardised in NIST SP 800-185. KMAC256 targets 256-bit security.

Resending a captured valid message, such as an authenticated payment request, so it takes effect again. MACs do not stop it; protocols include a timestamp, counter or nonce in the authenticated data and reject repeats.
example: Resending yesterday's "refund issued" webhook with its genuine tag is a replay.

definition: Assurance that a message is new rather than a replay, usually from a timestamp, sequence number or nonce inside the authenticated data.
Information leaked by how a computation runs rather than by its output, such as timing, power use, cache behaviour or error messages. Many practical crypto breaks are side channels.
An online payments provider whose webhooks carry a Stripe-Signature header: an HMAC-SHA256 over a timestamp and the body, so receivers can reject old events.

The scheme AWS uses to authenticate API requests: an HMAC-SHA256 over a canonical form of the request, with a signing key derived by chaining HMACs over the date, region and service. SigV4a is an asymmetric variant.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud computing platform.

JSON Web Signature represents arbitrary payloads protected by a digital signature or MAC; it is not limited to JWT claims. The usual compact form encodes rather than encrypts its payload, so anyone holding the token can normally read it.

JSON Web Encryption represents encrypted content, which can contain JWT claims or other application data. It provides the specified encryption and authentication properties, subject to correct algorithm selection and key handling.
The JWT algorithm "HMAC with SHA-256": tokens are authenticated with a shared secret, so anyone able to verify can also mint tokens.

Asymmetric JWT algorithms: RS256 uses RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with SHA-256; ES256 uses ECDSA on P-256 with SHA-256. Verification needs the public key, while signing needs the private key; a public verification key alone should not enable practical forgery under the scheme’s assumptions.

An encoding that writes binary data using 64 printable characters (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /), 6 bits per character, padded with =. It is reversible by anyone and gives no secrecy. The base64url variant swaps + and / for - and _ so the result is safe in URLs.
example: 32 random bytes become 43 base64url characters (without padding).

definition: A cookie whose contents carry a MAC so the server can detect tampering. Signing does not hide the contents, and it is not the same as encrypting the cookie.
Popular Python web frameworks. Both offer cryptographically signed cookies keyed by the application's SECRET_KEY.

A composition that authenticates an unambiguously encoded ciphertext, IV and required context, using a key separate from encryption. Under suitable primitive and protocol assumptions, checking that tag before decryption prevents a padding-validity oracle on unauthenticated ciphertext.
example: IPsec ESP and TLS's RFC 7366 extension use encrypt-then-MAC.

definition: Computing a MAC over the plaintext, then encrypting plaintext and tag together. The receiver must decrypt before checking, which enabled padding-oracle attacks such as Lucky Thirteen on TLS CBC suites.
Encrypting the plaintext and separately sending a MAC of the plaintext. The deterministic tag reveals when two messages are equal, and decryption happens before verification; original SSH used it.

A suite of protocols for securing IP traffic. Encapsulating Security Payload can provide confidentiality, integrity and origin authentication according to the selected suite; RFC 4303 also permits particular confidentiality-only or authentication-only configurations.

Using distinct keys for distinct purposes, directions or contexts, often derived with explicit labels. This reduces unintended interaction between uses; it does not guarantee that every weakness in one part of a system is isolated.
The property that doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. Webhook handlers record processed event IDs so retries and replays do not repeat side effects.

A time representation based on elapsed nominal seconds since the start of 1 January 1970 UTC, with a specified treatment of leap seconds. Unix-style webhook timestamps commonly use this epoch; follow the provider’s format and units.

Cryptography using a related public and private key pair. Public-key encryption lets senders encrypt to a recipient; signatures let a private signing key produce proofs checked with a public key. The public key still needs authenticated binding to its intended owner.
example: Anyone can encrypt to Bob with his RSA public key; only his private key decrypts.

definition: A function designed to be easy to compute but computationally hard to invert without specified secret information, under its security assumptions and appropriate parameters. The RSA permutation is an example; tiny textbook parameters do not provide that hardness.

Splitting a whole number into the primes that multiply to give it. Multiplying two large primes is easy, but recovering them from the product is believed hard for classical computers; RSA depends on that.
example: A correctly generated RSA-2048 modulus uses two large independent primes; weak or shared primes can make a nominally 2048-bit key easy to factor.

definition: An integer that is a product of two primes, which may be equal by the mathematical definition. Ordinary two-prime RSA uses distinct primes; PKCS #1 also specifies multi-prime RSA, whose modulus has more than two prime factors.
example: 3233 = 61 × 53 is a semiprime.

definition: The general number field sieve, the best known general-purpose classical method for factoring large RSA-like integers. Its commonly quoted subexponential complexity is a heuristic expected-work model, not a proven runtime bound for every input.
example: The RSA-250 report lists about 2,450 core-years of sieving, 250 of linear algebra and 114 of polynomial selection; these are historical reported costs.

definition: A 250-decimal-digit (829-bit) number from the RSA Factoring Challenge, factored in February 2020 by Boudot and colleagues with the number field sieve.

Arithmetic in which numbers wrap around after reaching a fixed number, the modulus, keeping only remainders. "a mod n" is the remainder when a is divided by n; RSA, Diffie–Hellman and elliptic curves all work this way.
example: 17 mod 5 = 2, just as 5 hours after 9 o'clock is 2 o'clock on a 12-hour clock.

definition: The positive integer defining modular remainders. Ordinary two-prime RSA uses the public product of two distinct secret primes; PKCS #1 also permits multi-prime RSA. The modulus bit length is the quoted RSA key size.
example: The toy RSA key has modulus 3233.

definition: Two numbers are congruent modulo n, written a ≡ b (mod n), when they leave the same remainder after dividing by n, that is, when n divides their difference.
example: 17 ≡ 2 (mod 5), because both leave remainder 2.

definition: Euler’s totient φ(n) counts the integers from 1 through n that are coprime to n. For the product of two distinct primes p and q, φ(n) is (p−1)(q−1); multi-prime RSA uses the corresponding product over all distinct prime factors.

The smallest positive exponent λ(n) for which every invertible residue modulo n raised to that exponent is 1. For two distinct odd primes p and q, λ(pq) is lcm(p−1,q−1); RSA’s public and private exponents are inverses modulo λ(n).
example: For p = 5, q = 11, λ(n) = lcm(4, 10) = 20 while φ(n) = 40.

definition: If m and n share no factor, then m^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). It is the step that makes RSA decryption undo encryption.
For a prime p and any number x not divisible by p, x^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). It lets exponents be reduced modulo p − 1 and is the prime-modulus case of Euler's theorem.

For pairwise coprime moduli, a system of remainders determines one unique remainder modulo their product. RSA can use separate calculations modulo its secret primes and combine them, but the actual speed-up depends on implementation and hardware.
The largest whole number that divides two numbers exactly. Euclid's algorithm computes it quickly even for 2,048-bit numbers; if two RSA moduli share a prime, their GCD reveals it.
The smallest positive number that is a multiple of each of two numbers.
Two numbers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is 1: they share no prime factor. RSA's public exponent must be coprime to φ(n).
example: 17 and 3120 are coprime.

definition: An algorithm computing the greatest common divisor of two integers and Bézout coefficients expressing that divisor as their integer linear combination. It yields a modular inverse when the value and modulus are coprime.
example: It finds d = 2753 with 17 × 2753 ≡ 1 (mod 3120).

definition: The number that, multiplied by a given number, leaves remainder 1 modulo n. It exists only when the two are coprime. In Python, pow(e, -1, n) computes it.
example: 2753 is the inverse of 17 modulo 3120.

definition: Computing a^b mod n efficiently by repeated squaring and multiplying, reducing modulo n after every step so numbers stay small. RSA and Diffie–Hellman are built on it; Python's pow(a, b, n) does it.

The exponent in an RSA public key, used by the public RSA operation. The common value 65537 has two set bits and supports efficient exponentiation; key generation must still check its required coprimality condition.

The secret exponent used by the private RSA operation. PKCS #1 requires it to invert the public exponent modulo the least common multiple of the prime factors minus one; the elementary totient-based recipe is a sufficient two-prime construction.
example: For the toy key with e = 17 and φ(n) = 3120, d = 2753.

definition: RSA used directly as c = m^e mod n with no padding. It is deterministic, malleable and leaks small messages, so it must never be used for real data.

Encryption that returns the same ciphertext for the same plaintext and key under the same other inputs. This reveals equality. With public-key encryption, an attacker can also encrypt guesses from a small candidate space; symmetric schemes do not automatically give an attacker that capability.
example: Textbook RSA encrypts 65 to 2790 every time.

definition: A randomised encoding applied to a message before the RSA operation. Modern encryption padding (OAEP) fixes textbook RSA's determinism and malleability.

Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding, specified for RSA in RFC 8017. It encodes a message using a random seed and hash-based masking, so repeated encryptions normally differ. Decryption rejects invalid encodings; this does not authenticate the sender or make every altered ciphertext invalid.
example: RSA-OAEP with a 3,072-bit key and SHA-256 can carry at most 318 bytes.

definition: The hash-based mask generation function used by OAEP and RSA-PSS. It hashes a seed with successive four-byte counters and has a specified maximum output of 2^32 hash lengths; it does not provide unbounded output.
The RSA standard from the Public-Key Cryptography Standards series, now RFC 8017. Its old v1.5 encryption padding is vulnerable to Bleichenbacher's attack; v2 adds OAEP.

Daniel Bleichenbacher's 1998 padding-oracle attack on PKCS #1 v1.5 RSA encryption: a server that reveals whether decrypted padding was valid lets an attacker decrypt ciphertexts with many adaptive queries.
"Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat" (2017): research showing many major vendors' TLS stacks were still vulnerable to Bleichenbacher's attack through RSA key transport.
The old TLS key exchange where the client encrypts a random premaster secret to the server's long-term RSA key. It has no forward secrecy and TLS 1.3 removed it.
example: A recorded TLS 1.2 RSA-key-transport session can be decrypted if the server key leaks years later.

definition: A design combining public-key establishment with symmetric authenticated encryption for data. RSA-OAEP can protect a generated data key; HPKE instead combines a KEM, KDF and AEAD. Envelope encryption can also wrap a data key under a symmetric master key.
example: Encrypt a 1 GB file with AES-GCM, then wrap the 32-byte AES key with the recipient's RSA-OAEP public key.

definition: A public-key primitive whose encapsulation algorithm outputs a shared key and ciphertext; the matching private key performs decapsulation. Confidentiality and correctness follow the scheme’s stated assumptions, validation and failure rules. ML-KEM is an example.
Hybrid Public Key Encryption (RFC 9180): a standard way to encrypt to a public key by combining a KEM, a KDF and an AEAD.
Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme: hybrid encryption to an elliptic-curve public key using an ephemeral ECDH exchange, a KDF, a cipher and a MAC.
Triple Data Encryption Algorithm (Triple DES): the old DES cipher applied three times. NIST disallows it for new encryption; it appears in key-size tables only for historical comparison.
A measure of attack cost in bits: "k-bit security" means the best known attack needs about 2^k operations. AES-128, RSA-3072 and 256-bit elliptic curves all target 128 bits.
example: RSA-2048 is rated at about 112-bit security by NIST SP 800-57.

definition: Elliptic-curve cryptography: public-key cryptography built on the group of points on an elliptic curve over a finite field. Because the best attacks are generic, 256-bit keys give about 128-bit security, matching 3,072-bit RSA.
example: X25519 key exchange and Ed25519 signatures are ECC.

definition: A nonsingular algebraic curve with a group law and a designated identity. In prime characteristic greater than three, a common short Weierstrass form uses a cubic in the horizontal coordinate; valid coefficients must avoid singularities. Finite-field implementations operate on discrete points, not a continuous drawing.
example: y² ≡ x³ + 2x + 2 (mod 17) has 19 points, including the point at infinity.

definition: A finite set of numbers where you can add, subtract, multiply and divide (except by zero), such as the whole numbers modulo a prime. Elliptic-curve and finite-field Diffie–Hellman cryptography work in finite fields.
example: The integers 0 to 16 with arithmetic modulo 17 form a finite field.

definition: The group operation combining two elliptic-curve points. The geometric chord-and-tangent picture includes doubling and the point at infinity; finite-field formulas implement the same algebraic rule and need the specified exceptional-case handling.

Multiplying a curve point by an integer using the group’s addition operation. Computing a public multiple is efficient; recovering a nonzero private scalar from its public point is intended to be hard for an appropriately chosen cryptographic subgroup.
example: On the toy curve, 3 × G = (10, 6) for G = (5, 1).

definition: The standard way to compute k × G: walk through k's bits, doubling the running point each step and adding G where the bit is 1. It takes about log₂(k) doublings, a few hundred for a 256-bit k.
The extra point O that acts as zero for elliptic-curve point addition: adding it to any point leaves that point unchanged. A generator's multiples reach it after (order) steps.
example: On the toy curve, 19 × G is the point at infinity.

definition: A fixed public element G of a group whose multiples (or powers) run through a large subgroup. ECC public keys are multiples of G; in Diffie–Hellman, g is the base that is raised to secret exponents.
example: The toy curve's generator (5, 1) has order 19.

definition: The order of an element is the least positive number of repeated group operations needed to reach the identity; a group’s order is its number of elements. DH and ECC protocols commonly select a subgroup of large prime order, although a full ambient group can have composite order.
example: 5 has order 22 modulo 23; 2 has order 11.

definition: A subset of a group that is a group by itself, such as all the powers of one element. The security of Diffie–Hellman depends on the size of the subgroup the generator produces, not just on the size of the prime.
example: The powers of 2 modulo 23 form an 11-element subgroup.

definition: The ratio between the number of points on an elliptic curve and the order of the prime subgroup actually used. Curve25519 has cofactor 8, so protocols must handle low-order points.

The elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem: given G and P = k × G, find k. No sub-exponential classical attack is known for well-chosen curves, so the best generic attack takes on the order of √(group order) steps, up to a small constant factor.

A low-memory generic discrete-logarithm algorithm with expected work on the order of the square root of the group order under its usual random-walk model. Constant factors depend on the variant. For an appropriate group of roughly 256-bit prime order, this suggests roughly 128-bit classical strength.
An elliptic curve over the prime 2^255 − 19, designed by Daniel J. Bernstein for fast, constant-time implementations. X25519 uses it in Montgomery form, and Ed25519 uses a related Edwards curve.

Different equation shapes for elliptic curves. Weierstrass form (y² = x³ + ax + b) is used by P-256; Montgomery form suits X25519's x-only key exchange; twisted Edwards form gives Ed25519 fast, complete addition formulas.

An EdDSA signature scheme specified in RFC 8032. The private signing scalar is derived from the secret seed; a separate per-message secret nonce scalar is derived deterministically from a secret prefix and the message. Fresh external randomness is not required for each signature, but secure seed generation and side-channel protection remain necessary.

A NIST prime-field elliptic curve also named secp256r1. It is specified for several cryptographic uses and has roughly 128-bit generic classical strength; whether it is approved or required depends on the protocol and policy.
The 256-bit elliptic curve used by Bitcoin and Ethereum for ECDSA signatures.

Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm. It requires a suitable secret per-message signing value, generated securely or derived by a standard deterministic procedure. Reusing that value across appropriate distinct-message signatures can reveal the private signing key.
A quantum algorithm that factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time. A large enough fault-tolerant quantum computer running it would break RSA, Diffie–Hellman and ECC.

The threat that adversaries record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists. It is why key exchange is being moved to post-quantum schemes first.
Public-key algorithms believed to resist attacks by quantum computers, such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key establishment and ML-DSA for signatures.

Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism, standardised by NIST in FIPS 203 (2024), derived from Kyber. Its parameter sets are ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024. The final standard differs from earlier Kyber implementations and is not a wire-compatible synonym.
example: Google announced a transition from Kyber768 plus X25519 to ML-KEM-768 plus X25519 for Chrome 131 in September 2024.

definition: A 2012 study that scanned internet hosts and factored tens of thousands of RSA keys from embedded devices whose keys shared primes because they were generated at boot with too little entropy.

A computer built into a product such as a router, camera or lock. Inadequate boot-time randomness and limited update support can cause security failures; the 2012 Mining your Ps and Qs study documented weak keys in some embedded-device populations.

A protocol (1976) letting two parties agree a shared secret over a public channel: each raises a public generator to a secret exponent, swaps the result, and raises the other's value to its own secret. It must be authenticated to stop a man in the middle.
example: With p = 23 and g = 5, secrets 6 and 15 give public values 8 and 19, and both sides compute 2.

definition: A protocol in which parties establish shared keying material across a communication channel. Authentication and key derivation must follow the specified protocol: raw Diffie–Hellman output normally enters a KDF, while a KEM already defines a shared-key output.

The secret value produced by a key-establishment scheme for both participants. Raw DH outputs require the specified key-derivation step; a KEM may already output a pseudorandom secret under its definition. Follow the protocol instead of treating all key-exchange outputs identically.
example: X25519 produces a 32-byte shared secret.

definition: Given g, p and A = g^a mod p, find the exponent a. For a well-chosen large group no efficient classical method is known, which protects Diffie–Hellman secrets; Shor's algorithm would solve it on a large quantum computer.
example: For p = 23, g = 5, A = 8, trying exponents finds a = 6; for 2,048-bit groups that is infeasible.

definition: In a chosen group, the assumption that computing the shared generator power from the two public powers is computationally infeasible. Turning that value into a secure session key additionally requires a suitable KDF and the security assumptions of the complete protocol.

An attacker observing traffic without changing it. Suitable DH parameters and secret exponents can hide the shared value under the chosen computational assumption, but unauthenticated DH does not resist active share substitution.
An attacker who can modify, inject, drop or replay messages, not just read them. Unauthenticated key exchange and unauthenticated encryption fall to active attackers.

An active attacker interposes between communicating parties and can establish separate exchanges with each. Authenticating the intended peers and binding their identities to the exchange protects against this attack under the protocol’s assumptions; compromised credentials or endpoints remain separate risks.
example: Mallory swaps her own DH value for Alice's and Bob's, ending up with one key shared with each.

definition: Key establishment that cryptographically authenticates the intended peer or peers according to the protocol. Authentication may be one-way or mutual; a valid computation alone does not verify a human identity without an appropriate trust binding.

A TLS 1.3 handshake message proving possession of the certificate’s signing key. Its signature covers a context-specific encoding including the handshake transcript hash; either a server or a certificate-authenticating client can send it.

A hash over a protocol’s specified handshake-message encoding. In TLS 1.3 it binds key derivation and authentication to the negotiation; its security requires the protocol’s authentication and Finished checks, not hashing alone.

A sequence of certificates used to build a validated path from an end-entity key toward an accepted trust anchor. Verifiers check signatures and policy constraints; a root trust anchor need not be transmitted in the server’s chain.
An organisation trusted to issue certificates binding public keys to identities such as domain names, by signing them.
example: Let's Encrypt is a certificate authority that issues free TLS certificates.

definition: Secure Shell, a protocol for authenticated encrypted remote access. Clients authenticate servers using configured trust, commonly a saved host key in known_hosts or a host certificate signed by a trusted authority; user authentication is a separate step.
Accepting a peer's key the first time you see it and then alerting if it ever changes, as SSH does with known_hosts. It cannot detect an attacker who is already present at first contact.

The end-to-end encryption protocol used by the Signal messenger (and WhatsApp), which mixes long-term identity keys into its key exchange and lets users compare "safety numbers" to detect a man in the middle.
example: Signal users can compare Safety Numbers through a trusted channel to help check the identity keys of their conversation.

definition: An algorithm evolving message keys through symmetric-key chains and periodic Diffie–Hellman contributions. Erasing old keys can protect past messages; recovery after compromise needs fresh secret input unavailable to the attacker. Continuous endpoint compromise defeats those guarantees.
A modern VPN protocol built on the Noise framework, using X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and BLAKE2s. Each peer is configured in advance with the other's static public key.

A framework specifying cryptographic handshake patterns and their security properties. Authentication, identity hiding and forward-secrecy properties depend on the chosen pattern, roles, keys and correct protocol use.

A long-lived cryptographic key, in contrast to an ephemeral key generated for a limited exchange or session. It can be an asymmetric identity key pair or, in relevant protocols, a symmetric pre-shared key.
A secret established between parties before the exchange that uses it. TLS 1.3 supports external PSKs and resumption PSKs, with profiles that can combine a PSK with fresh Diffie–Hellman exchange.

A prime p of the form 2q + 1 with q also prime. For cryptographic-sized p and q, the nonzero residues modulo p have a large order-q subgroup; the possible subgroup orders divide 2q. The toy prime 23 has q=11.
example: 23 = 2 × 11 + 1 is a safe prime.

definition: An attack that supplies a value in a small-order subgroup to extract information about a victim’s secret through its responses. Defences depend on the protocol and group, including specified public-value validation, cofactor handling and rejection of invalid shared outputs.
example: Sending 22 (that is, −1 modulo 23) forces the secret to be 1 or 22.

definition: An attack on elliptic-curve code that accepts a received public point without checking that it lies on the intended curve. The usual point-arithmetic formulas then quietly compute on a different curve the attacker chose, often one with small subgroups, so responses made with a reused private scalar can leak it piece by piece. Validating each received point against the curve equation, as the scheme's standard requires, prevents it.
example: A service that multiplies an unchecked (x, y) pair by its long-term ECDH private key can be fed points from weak curves until the key is recovered.

definition: Python's built-in exception for an argument of the right type but an unacceptable value. In the `cryptography` library, an X25519 `exchange` whose result would be an all-zero shared secret raises it; code should treat that as a failed handshake, not substitute a default value.
example: Passing a low-order X25519 public key to `exchange` raises `ValueError: Error computing shared key.` in cryptography 50.

definition: Checks required by a particular key scheme and protocol before accepting peer values. A finite-field prime-order profile may check range and subgroup membership; X25519 instead has its own decoding rules, with an all-zero-result check required by protocols such as TLS 1.3.

A 2015 attack showing that many TLS servers accepted 512-bit export-grade Diffie–Hellman, which an active attacker could force and break, and that a few shared 1,024-bit primes made nation-state precomputation plausible.
Deliberately weakened cryptography (such as 512-bit DH or 40-bit keys) that 1990s US export rules permitted. Servers that kept supporting it were later exploited through downgrade attacks.
An active attack that tricks two parties into using an older or weaker protocol version or cipher than both support, then breaks the weak choice.
example: Logjam downgraded TLS connections to 512-bit export-grade DH.

definition: The named finite-field Diffie–Hellman groups for TLS standardised in RFC 7919 (ffdhe2048 and larger), built from vetted safe primes.

Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman: the same protocol as Diffie–Hellman but with scalar multiplication of curve points instead of modular exponentiation. Each side sends its secret times G and both compute (a × b) × G.
example: X25519 is ECDH on Curve25519.

definition: The key-agreement function over Curve25519 specified in RFC 7748, with 32-byte public and output encodings. It targets roughly 128-bit classical strength; authentication and key derivation belong to the surrounding protocol.
ECDH on Curve448 (RFC 7748), with 56-byte public keys and about 224-bit classical security. It is the higher-security sibling of X25519.

A key used for a limited exchange or session instead of as a long-term identity key. Fresh securely generated DH key pairs, appropriate authentication and erasure can provide forward secrecy against later compromise of long-term keys.

The property that stealing a long-term key later does not expose past sessions, because each session key came from ephemeral secrets that were erased. TLS 1.3 requires it for certificate-based handshakes.
example: If a 2024 authenticated session used fresh ephemeral secrets that were erased, later theft of its long-term identity key need not reveal the recorded session under the scheme’s security assumptions.

definition: The HKDF-based derivation in RFC 8446 that combines the selected PSK and/or (EC)DHE inputs, transcript hashes and purpose labels into handshake, application and exporter secrets. Exact inputs depend on the negotiated exchange profile.

Key establishment combining components such as X25519 and ML-KEM. A properly constructed combiner can retain secrecy if one component remains secure under its assumptions; correct authentication and endpoint security remain necessary.
example: In September 2024 Google announced a transition to X25519 combined with ML-KEM-768 for Chrome 131.

definition: Content delivery network: geographically distributed infrastructure serving or caching content close to users. Some CDNs terminate TLS and have reported deployments of hybrid post-quantum key establishment; neither property defines every CDN.
The process by which two Bluetooth devices establish shared keys. Its protection against a man in the middle depends on the association mode, such as comparing a numeric code shown on both devices.

A source of random or pseudorandom values. Secret keys and tokens need a generator with appropriate cryptographic unpredictability; some public cryptographic nonces instead use a coordinated deterministic counter.

Pseudorandom number generator: an algorithm that expands a seed into a long sequence that looks random. Statistical PRNGs like Python's random are fine for simulations but predictable, so never for secrets.

A pseudorandom generator intended to make output computationally unpredictable under specified assumptions about its seed and implementation. State compromise, recovery and past-output protection need separate analysis. Use the operating system’s supported cryptographic randomness API.
example: secrets.token_bytes(32) returns 32 bytes from the OS CSPRNG.

definition: The deterministic statistical generator used by Python’s random module. Its state includes 624 stored 32-bit words and an index; observing 624 consecutive complete outputs from an unchanged stream can recover predictive state. Truncated or interleaved observations need different analysis.

An initial input setting a pseudorandom generator’s state. A CSPRNG needs sufficient unpredictable entropy. A fully known deterministic state permits prediction until fresh secret entropy is incorporated; reseeding and state management depend on the design.

Operating-system APIs for secure random values, including Linux getrandom, BSD-family getentropy or arc4random, and Windows BCryptGenRandom. Availability, initialisation and error rules depend on the platform; application libraries normally wrap the appropriate API.

Python’s secrets module provides secure token and random-choice functions using the operating system’s secure randomness. The separate os.urandom function also returns operating-system random bytes; neither is the predictable random module.
example: secrets.token_urlsafe(32) encodes 32 random bytes as a 43-character URL-safe token without padding.

definition: A 2008 vulnerability in which a Debian-specific change to OpenSSL removed most of its random seeding, so keys generated on affected systems came from a tiny predictable set and had to be replaced.

The fail0verflow group’s 2010 analysis of a PlayStation 3 signing system found a repeated ECDSA per-message secret value. For two distinct message hashes signed with one private key and the same such value, the signing equations can reveal that key; this is not a claim about every Sony signing system.

An Informational RFC specifying deterministic generation of per-message secret values for DSA and ECDSA from the private key and message hash. It avoids needing fresh external randomness for every signature, but secure key generation and implementation remain necessary.
Key derivation function: turns a secret into one or more keys. HKDF suits secrets that already have high entropy; password KDFs such as Argon2id are deliberately slow for guessable passwords.

The HMAC-based extract-and-expand KDF in RFC 5869. It derives a pseudorandom key from suitable input and expands it with context labels into at most 255 hash lengths per Expand invocation. It is fast and does not harden guessable passwords.
example: TLS 1.3 derives all its traffic keys with HKDF.

definition: Pseudorandom key: the output of HKDF's Extract step, one hash length long, used as the key for the Expand step.
HKDF's names for its input secret (input keying material, such as a DH shared secret) and its output bytes (output keying material, the derived keys).

The context information passed to HKDF-Expand to bind output to an application, purpose or role. Distinct unambiguously encoded labels support key separation under HKDF’s assumptions; they do not add missing input entropy.
The standard for servers to send encrypted push messages to browsers; its encryption derives keys with ECDH and HKDF (RFC 8291).
A block cipher designed by Bruce Schneier in 1993 whose expensive key setup bcrypt repeats to make hashing slow.
An open competition (2013–2015) to select a new password-hashing function; Argon2 won.
The self-describing text format for stored password hashes, such as $argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$salt$hash, recording the algorithm, version, parameters and salt alongside the hash.
Upgrading a stored password hash to new parameters or a new algorithm the next time the user logs in successfully, when the plaintext password is briefly available.

Hardware security module: a device designed to protect cryptographic keys and perform controlled operations with them. Tamper resistance, export rules and validation depend on the particular device and configuration; it is not a guarantee that keys can never leave.
Application-specific integrated circuit: a chip built for one task, such as computing a particular hash extremely fast. Memory-hard functions blunt ASIC and GPU cracking.

Random-access memory: a computer’s working memory. Password-hashing memory cost is set by the selected algorithm and parameters; memory hardness does not imply every valid setting uses tens of megabytes.

A version 1 UUID uses a timestamp, clock sequence and node identifier. The node identifier may come from a MAC address or a generated alternative; UUIDv1 is not designed as an unpredictable secret token.

A media access control address identifies an interface on a local network; it is unrelated to a message authentication code. Addresses may be assigned, locally administered or randomised rather than immutable hardware identities.
A unit of memory equal to 1,024 bytes (2^10). Argon2 expresses its memory parameter m in KiB.
example: m=65536 means 65,536 KiB = 64 MiB.

definition: A unit of data equal to 10^9 bytes (often used loosely for 2^30 bytes).
One thousandth of a second. Password hashes are often tuned to take tens to hundreds of milliseconds.

Secure Sockets Layer: the obsolete predecessor of TLS. SSL 2.0 and SSL 3.0 are prohibited by their relevant IETF specifications; whether a particular installed system has disabled them is a configuration question.

The TLS version specified in RFC 8446 (2018). It uses AEAD record protection and PSK and/or ephemeral (EC)DHE key exchange, removes RSA key transport, and derives keys with an HKDF-based key schedule.
The widely used Python package "cryptography", which offers high-level recipes such as Fernet and lower-level "hazardous materials" (hazmat) primitives such as AESGCM and X25519.

Core software managing a computer’s resources, such as Linux, Windows or macOS. Cryptographic applications use its secure-random APIs; entropy sources, initialisation and random-generator internals depend on the platform.
Portable Document Format, a document file format. Its flexible structure made it a convenient carrier for the SHAttered SHA-1 collision.
A copy of a database's contents, for example from a backup or a SQL injection. Password hashes in it can be attacked offline.

A secret authorising a password reset, normally delivered in a link. It should be unpredictable, expire according to policy, be accepted only once and be stored securely, commonly as a digest. Protect the delivery and redemption paths as well.

A system that collects monitoring data (metrics, logs and events) from many devices or services and forwards it for storage and analysis. High message volumes make per-key message limits, such as GCM nonce limits, a real concern.

The memory-hard password-hashing family that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition. Argon2d uses data-dependent memory access, Argon2i uses data-independent access, and Argon2id combines both access strategies. RFC 9106 specifies the family.

Processing intended to prevent people being identified, considering reasonably likely means of identification. Replacing an identifier with a predictable hash can leave it linkable or recoverable, so it is not automatically anonymisation.

An integer used to multiply a curve point through repeated group addition. A private ECC scalar is chosen from the range required by the scheme; it is different from a scalar measurement in ordinary algebra.

A Python interface to Argon2 with a high-level PasswordHasher API. It stores algorithm parameters and a random salt with each hash, verifies stored records and can identify records needing an upgrade.

A family of signature schemes using twisted Edwards curves and deterministic signing-value derivation. RFC 8032 specifies Ed25519 and Ed448 plus their context and prehash variants; the family name is not another name for Ed25519 alone.

An input to HKDF-Extract, normally public and independent of the input keying material. RFC 5869 uses one hash-output length of zero bytes when it is absent. It has a different role from a per-password storage salt and must meet the surrounding protocol’s assumptions.
The Networking and Cryptography library, designed to provide high-level cryptographic operations. libsodium is a separate library derived from NaCl; the names do not identify the same implementation.
The message-format standard for encrypted and signed messages, specified in RFC 9580. GnuPG is one implementation; OpenPGP names the standard rather than that particular tool.

Two positive integers are non-coprime when their greatest common divisor exceeds 1. They have a shared prime factor; a value non-coprime to a positive modulus greater than 1 has no multiplicative inverse modulo that modulus.

The CRYSTALS-Kyber lattice-based key-encapsulation proposal from which NIST derived ML-KEM. Earlier Kyber deployments and the final ML-KEM standard have differences and cannot be treated as wire-compatible names for one format.

Systems of connected devices that interact with the physical world through sensing or actuation. Many contain embedded computers, but an embedded device need not be network-connected or part of the Internet of Things.
A family of sponge-based cryptographic functions underlying SHA-3. Ethereum uses Keccak-256 with domain padding different from standard SHA3-256, so their 256-bit digests are not interchangeable.

The fixed chunk of data a block cipher or hash function processes in one step. AES always works on 128-bit (16-byte) blocks; SHA-256 processes 64-byte message blocks, which is also the block size HMAC-SHA256 fits its key to. scrypt's separate block-size parameter, r, instead sets the size of its internal mixing blocks (128 × r bytes) and so scales its memory use.
example: A 10-byte message encrypted with AES-CBC is padded to one 16-byte block; an HMAC-SHA256 key longer than 64 bytes is hashed first.
